fine_trace.note: Attacker-controlled input bytes are read from the buffer; when the first 4 bytes equal "bFLT" (line 259: !memcmp (tmp, "bFLT", 4)) the bflt bin plugin is selected and its load() is invoked.
The 64-byte bFLT header, including the attacker-controlled revision field, is read into bhdr and parsed with r_read_be32.

Admission: the revision must equal FLAT_VERSION (4), otherwise bflt_init_hdr fails and r_bin_bflt_new_buf frees the object before any list is cached; with rev == 4 the header is stored (bin->hdr = p_hdr) and load() succeeds.
r_bin_object_set_items invokes the bflt plugin relocs() (default filter_rules = UT64_MAX); a new RList is allocated for the relocation entries.

Root cause: the freshly allocated list is cached in the bflt object while the identical pointer is returned to r_bin_object_set_items, which takes ownership and frees it. obj->relocs_list is left dangling; the safety condition that should hold is that the object retains no pointer to the transferred list (obj->relocs_list == NULL) when r_bin_bflt_free runs.

The caller converts the returned list into an rbtree (bo->relocs) and frees the RList structure (with l->free = NULL), so the memory pointed to by obj->relocs_list is freed while the bflt object still references it.

Sink: when the bin file is freed, r_bin_file_free -> plugin destroy -> r_bin_bflt_free calls r_list_free on the already-freed list; r_list_purge reads list->head from freed memory -> heap-use-after-free READ 8 (crash state: r_list_free <- r_bin_bflt_free <- r_bin_file_free).
